notes.title: Ex-8.1: Speed, Distance and Time
notes.summary: Basic Question of math and science
notes.contentHtml:
1. Basic Definitions

1. Distance

Distance is the total length covered by a moving object.

Example: A boy cycles 5 km from his home to school. The distance covered is 5 km.

2. Time

Time is the duration taken to cover a distance.

Example: A boy takes 30 minutes to reach school. The time taken is 30 minutes.

3. Speed

Speed tells us how fast or slowly an object moves. It is the distance travelled per unit of time.

Example: A car travels 60 km in 2 hours.

Speed = Distance ÷ Time

Speed = 60 ÷ 2 = 30 km/h

2. Speed, Distance and Time Formula
Quantity	Formula
Speed	Distance ÷ Time
Distance	Speed × Time
Time	Distance ÷ Speed

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/czb80riv/image/upload/v1792043420/studysathi/uploads/xfu9dsqjf22mdm13xrv8.jpg)

Solved Example 1: Find the distance.

A car travels at 40 km/h for 3 hours. Find the distance covered.

Formula:

Distance = Speed × Time

Solution:

Distance = 40 × 3

Answer: 120 km

Solved Example 2: Find the time.

A cyclist travels 20 km at 10 km/h. Find the time taken.

Formula:

Time = Distance ÷ Speed

Solution:

Time = 20 ÷ 10

Answer: 2 hours

3. Conversion of Speed Units

There are two important conversions.

A. Convert km/h into m/s

Multiply the speed by 5/18.

$$ \text{Speed in m/s}=\text{Speed in km/h}\times\frac{5}{18} $$

Solved Example: Convert 72 km/h into m/s.

$$ 72\times\frac{5}{18} $$ $$ =4\times5 $$

Answer: 20 m/s

B. Convert m/s into km/h

Multiply the speed by 18/5.

$$ \text{Speed in km/h}=\text{Speed in m/s}\times\frac{18}{5} $$

Solved Example: Convert 25 m/s into km/h.

$$ 25\times\frac{18}{5} $$ $$ =5\times18 $$

Answer: 90 km/h

Remember:

km/h → m/s: Multiply by 5/18.
m/s → km/h: Multiply by 18/5.
4. Conversion of Time

When speed is given in km/h, time should generally be expressed in hours.

Minutes	Hours
15 minutes	15/60 = 1/4 hour
30 minutes	30/60 = 1/2 hour
45 minutes	45/60 = 3/4 hour
60 minutes	60/60 = 1 hour
90 minutes	90/60 = 3/2 hours

Solved Example: Convert 90 minutes into hours.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{90}{60}=1.5\text{ hours} $$

Answer: 1.5 hours

5. Average Speed

Average speed is calculated by dividing the total distance travelled by the total time taken.

$$ \boxed{\text{Average Speed}=\frac{\text{Total Distance}}{\text{Total Time}}} $$

Solved Example 1

A car travels 120 km in 2 hours and another 180 km in 3 hours. Find its average speed.

Step 1: Total distance

120 + 180 = 300 km

Step 2: Total time

2 + 3 = 5 hours

Step 3: Average speed

$$ \text{Average Speed}=\frac{300}{5} $$

Answer: 60 km/h

Solved Example 2: Equal Distances

A car travels equal distances at 40 km/h and 60 km/h. Find its average speed.

When the distances are equal, use:

$$ \boxed{\text{Average Speed}=\frac{2xy}{x+y}} $$

Here, x = 40 and y = 60.

$$ =\frac{2\times40\times60}{40+60} $$ $$ =\frac{4800}{100} $$

Answer: 48 km/h

Important: Do not simply calculate the average of two speeds when finding average speed for a journey. Use the total distance divided by the total time, or the special formula when the distances are equal.

6. Quick Revision: Important Formulas
No.	Formula
1	Speed = Distance ÷ Time
2	Distance = Speed × Time
3	Time = Distance ÷ Speed
4	km/h to m/s = Multiply by 5/18
5	m/s to km/h = Multiply by 18/5
6	Average speed = Total distance ÷ Total time
7	Average speed for two equal distances = 2xy ÷ (x + y)
Important Points to Remember
Always write the correct formula before solving a problem.
Convert minutes into hours when necessary.
Convert speed units carefully.
Use the correct unit in the final answer.
For average speed, calculate total distance and total time first.
Use the special average-speed formula only when the distances are equal.

notes.title: Exercise 8.2 — Detailed Notes, Formulas, Quick Tricks & Solved Questions
notes.summary: These notes follow your uploaded Discover Mathematics, Class 8, Volume 2 textbook. Exercise 8.2 covers train problems, relative speed, boats and streams, and problems involving different travel times.
notes.contentHtml:
1. Train Problems 🚆
Concept 1: When a train crosses a pole

When a train crosses a pole, the train covers a distance equal to its own length.

Important formulas
$$ \boxed{\text{Speed}=\frac{\text{Length of Train}}{\text{Time}}} $$ $$ \boxed{\text{Time}=\frac{\text{Length of Train}}{\text{Speed}}} $$ $$ \boxed{\text{Length of Train}=\text{Speed}\times\text{Time}} $$

Important: If the train's length is in metres and time is in seconds, calculate speed in metres per second (m/s).

![Fig: Screenshot 2026 10 15 113033](https://res.cloudinary.com/czb80riv/image/upload/v1792044075/studysathi/uploads/xqicjk6qqvxabiupkdjl.png)

Solved Example

A train is 150 m long. It crosses a pole in 10 seconds. Find its speed.

Step 1: Write the given values.

Length = 150 m

Time = 10 seconds

Step 2: Apply the formula.

$$ \text{Speed}=\frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Time}} $$ $$ =\frac{150}{10}=15\text{ m/s} $$

Step 3: Convert into km/h.

$$ 15\times\frac{18}{5}=54\text{ km/h} $$

Answer: 15 m/s or 54 km/h.

Quick Trick

Whenever a question says “a train crosses a pole”, use:

Distance = Length of train.

2. When a Train Crosses a Bridge or Platform

When a train crosses a bridge or platform, it must travel the length of the bridge or platform plus its own length.

5
Important formula
$$ \boxed{\text{Total Distance}=\text{Train Length}+\text{Bridge Length}} $$

Therefore,

$$ \boxed{\text{Time}=\frac{\text{Train Length}+\text{Bridge Length}}{\text{Speed}}} $$
Solved Example

A train is 200 m long and crosses a bridge 300 m long. If its speed is 25 m/s, find the time taken.

Step 1: Find the total distance.

$$ 200+300=500\text{ m} $$

Step 2: Calculate the time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{500}{25} $$ $$ \boxed{20\text{ seconds}} $$
Quick Trick
Crossing a pole → use the train's length.
Crossing a bridge → add the train's length and bridge's length.
Crossing a platform → add the train's length and platform's length.

Common mistake: Do not use only the bridge's length when calculating the time taken by a train to cross the entire bridge.

3. Conversion of Speed

Before solving train problems, you may need to convert km/h into m/s.

Formula 1: km/h to m/s
$$ \boxed{\text{m/s}=\text{km/h}\times\frac{5}{18}} $$
Formula 2: m/s to km/h
$$ \boxed{\text{km/h}=\text{m/s}\times\frac{18}{5}} $$
Example

Convert 72 km/h into m/s.

$$ 72\times\frac{5}{18} =4\times5 $$ $$ \boxed{20\text{ m/s}} $$

Quick tip: If a train's length is given in metres and its crossing time in seconds, converting its speed into m/s usually makes the calculation easier.

4. Relative Speed

Relative speed tells us how quickly one moving object approaches or moves away from another.

There are two important cases.

Case A: Two objects move in the same direction

Subtract their speeds.

$$ \boxed{\text{Relative Speed}=\text{Faster Speed}-\text{Slower Speed}} $$
Example

Two trains move in the same direction at 60 km/h and 40 km/h.

$$ \text{Relative Speed}=60-40 $$ $$ \boxed{20\text{ km/h}} $$
Case B: Two objects move in opposite directions

Add their speeds.

$$ \boxed{\text{Relative Speed}=\text{Speed}_1+\text{Speed}_2} $$
Example

Two trains move towards each other at 60 km/h and 40 km/h.

$$ \text{Relative Speed}=60+40 $$ $$ \boxed{100\text{ km/h}} $$
Quick Trick
Direction	Operation
Same direction	Subtract
Opposite directions	Add

Remember: If you calculate the time taken for two trains to cross each other, you must also consider the lengths of both trains.

5. Two Trains Crossing Each Other

When two trains cross each other completely, the total distance covered relative to each other equals the sum of their lengths.

Case A: Same direction
$$ \boxed{\text{Time}=\frac{\text{Sum of Train Lengths}}{\text{Difference of Speeds}}} $$

The speeds must be expressed in the same units.

Case B: Opposite directions
$$ \boxed{\text{Time}=\frac{\text{Sum of Train Lengths}}{\text{Sum of Speeds}}} $$
Solved Example

Two trains are 100 m and 150 m long. They travel in opposite directions at 10 m/s and 15 m/s. Find the time taken to cross each other.

Step 1: Calculate the total length.

$$ 100+150=250\text{ m} $$

Step 2: Calculate the relative speed.

Since they move in opposite directions:

$$ 10+15=25\text{ m/s} $$

Step 3: Calculate the time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{250}{25} $$ $$ \boxed{10\text{ seconds}} $$
6. Boats and Streams 🚣

A boat's speed changes depending on whether it moves with or against the current.

Speed of the boat in still water: The speed of the boat when the water is not flowing.

Speed of the stream: The speed at which the water flows.

Case A: Downstream

Downstream means the boat moves in the same direction as the water current.

The current helps the boat move faster.

$$ \boxed{\text{Downstream Speed}=u+v} $$

Here:

\(u\) = speed of the boat in still water
\(v\) = speed of the stream
Example

Speed of the boat in still water = 10 km/h.

Speed of the stream = 2 km/h.

$$ \text{Downstream Speed}=10+2 $$ $$ \boxed{12\text{ km/h}} $$
Case B: Upstream

Upstream means the boat moves against the direction of the water current.

The current slows the boat down.

$$ \boxed{\text{Upstream Speed}=u-v} $$
Example

Speed of the boat in still water = 10 km/h.

Speed of the stream = 2 km/h.

$$ \text{Upstream Speed}=10-2 $$ $$ \boxed{8\text{ km/h}} $$
Two additional formulas

If downstream and upstream speeds are known:

$$ \boxed{\text{Boat Speed in Still Water}=\frac{D+U}{2}} $$ $$ \boxed{\text{Stream Speed}=\frac{D-U}{2}} $$

Here, \(D\) is the downstream speed and \(U\) is the upstream speed.

Quick Trick

Downstream = Add (+)

Upstream = Subtract (−)

7. Time, Speed and Distance in Boat Problems

The same basic formula applies to boats.

$$ \boxed{\text{Time}=\frac{\text{Distance}}{\text{Speed}}} $$

However, always use the correct speed.

For downstream travel, use downstream speed.
For upstream travel, use upstream speed.
Solved Example

A boat travels at 8 km/h in still water. The stream flows at 2 km/h. Find the time taken to travel 30 km downstream.

Step 1: Find downstream speed.

$$ 8+2=10\text{ km/h} $$

Step 2: Find time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{30}{10} $$ $$ \boxed{3\text{ hours}} $$
Another Example

A boat travels at 8 km/h in still water. The stream flows at 2 km/h. Find the time taken to travel 30 km upstream.

Step 1: Find upstream speed.

$$ 8-2=6\text{ km/h} $$

Step 2: Find time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{30}{6} $$ $$ \boxed{5\text{ hours}} $$

Notice that the same distance takes longer upstream because the water current opposes the boat's movement.

8. Questions Involving Being Late or Early

These questions compare the travel time at two different speeds.

The important idea is that the difference between the two travel times can be calculated from the difference between the late and early arrival times.

Example

A student is 10 minutes late when travelling at 4 km/h but arrives 10 minutes early when travelling at 6 km/h. Find the distance between home and school.

Step 1: Find the difference in travel times.

One journey makes the student 10 minutes late; the other makes the student 10 minutes early.

Therefore, the difference is:

$$ 10+10=20\text{ minutes} $$

Convert into hours:

$$ 20/60=\frac13\text{ hour} $$

Step 2: Let the distance be \(x\) km.

Time at 4 km/h:

$$ \frac{x}{4} $$

Time at 6 km/h:

$$ \frac{x}{6} $$

Step 3: Find the difference between the times.

$$ \frac{x}{4}-\frac{x}{6}=\frac13 $$

Taking the LCM of 4 and 6:

$$ \frac{3x-2x}{12}=\frac13 $$ $$ \frac{x}{12}=\frac13 $$ $$ x=4 $$

Answer: 4 km

Quick Trick

When a person is late at a slower speed and early at a faster speed:

Time difference = Late time + Early time

Convert the time difference into hours if the speeds are in km/h.

9. Exercise 8.2 — Detailed Solutions

The following questions are from Exercise 8.2 in your uploaded textbook.

Question 1

A train 150 m long crosses a pole in 12 seconds. Find its speed in m/s and km/h.

Given:

Train length = 150 m

Time = 12 seconds

Step 1: Calculate speed in m/s.

$$ \text{Speed}=\frac{150}{12}=12.5\text{ m/s} $$

Step 2: Convert into km/h.

$$ 12.5\times\frac{18}{5}=45\text{ km/h} $$

Answer: 12.5 m/s and 45 km/h.

Question 2

A train running at 72 km/h crosses a pole in 15 seconds. Find the length of the train.

Step 1: Convert speed into m/s.

$$ 72\times\frac{5}{18}=20\text{ m/s} $$

Step 2: Calculate the train's length.

$$ \text{Length}=\text{Speed}\times\text{Time} $$ $$ =20\times15 $$

Answer: 300 m.

Question 3

A train crosses a pole in 8 seconds and a bridge 120 m long in 20 seconds. Find the length of the train and its speed in km/h.

Let the train's length be \(x\) metres.

Step 1: Express the speed using the pole.

$$ \text{Speed}=\frac{x}{8}\text{ m/s} $$

Step 2: Express the speed using the bridge.

Total distance while crossing the bridge:

$$ x+120 $$

Therefore:

$$ \text{Speed}=\frac{x+120}{20}\text{ m/s} $$

Both expressions represent the same speed.

$$ \frac{x}{8}=\frac{x+120}{20} $$

Cross-multiply:

$$ 20x=8(x+120) $$ $$ 20x=8x+960 $$ $$ 12x=960 $$ $$ x=80 $$

The train's length is 80 m.

Step 3: Find its speed.

$$ \text{Speed}=\frac{80}{8}=10\text{ m/s} $$

Convert into km/h:

$$ 10\times\frac{18}{5}=36\text{ km/h} $$

Answer: Length = 80 m; speed = 36 km/h.

Question 4

A train 180 m long crosses a pole in 9 seconds. Find the time taken to cross a bridge 270 m long.

Step 1: Find the train's speed.

$$ \text{Speed}=\frac{180}{9}=20\text{ m/s} $$

Step 2: Find the total distance.

$$ 180+270=450\text{ m} $$

Step 3: Calculate time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{450}{20} $$ $$ \boxed{22.5\text{ seconds}} $$

Answer: 22.5 seconds.

Question 5

A man is 15 minutes late to catch a train when he cycles at 8 km/h but becomes 15 minutes early when he cycles at 12 km/h. Find the distance to the station.

Step 1: Calculate the difference in time.

$$ 15+15=30\text{ minutes} $$

Convert into hours:

$$ 30/60=\frac12\text{ hour} $$

Step 2: Let the distance be \(x\) km.

At 8 km/h, time taken:

$$ \frac{x}{8} $$

At 12 km/h, time taken:

$$ \frac{x}{12} $$

Step 3: Form the equation.

$$ \frac{x}{8}-\frac{x}{12}=\frac12 $$

LCM of 8 and 12 = 24.

$$ \frac{3x-2x}{24}=\frac12 $$ $$ \frac{x}{24}=\frac12 $$ $$ x=12 $$

Answer: 12 km.

Question 6

The speed of a boat in still water is 7 km/h. It travels 22 km upstream in 4 hours. Find the speed of the current.

Step 1: Calculate upstream speed.

$$ \text{Upstream Speed}=\frac{22}{4}=5.5\text{ km/h} $$

Step 2: Calculate the speed of the current.

$$ \text{Upstream Speed}=\text{Boat Speed}-\text{Stream Speed} $$

Therefore:

$$ 5.5=7-v $$ $$ v=7-5.5 $$

Answer: 1.5 km/h.

Question 7

A boat travels at 36 km/h in still water. It covers 56 km upstream in 1 hour 45 minutes. Find the time taken to cover the same distance downstream.

Step 1: Convert time into hours.

$$ 1\text{ hour }45\text{ minutes}=1.75\text{ hours} $$

Step 2: Calculate upstream speed.

$$ \text{Upstream Speed}=\frac{56}{1.75}=32\text{ km/h} $$

Step 3: Calculate the speed of the stream.

$$ \text{Stream Speed}=36-32=4\text{ km/h} $$

Step 4: Calculate downstream speed.

$$ 36+4=40\text{ km/h} $$

Step 5: Calculate downstream time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{56}{40}=1.4\text{ hours} $$

Convert 0.4 hour into minutes:

$$ 0.4\times60=24\text{ minutes} $$

Answer: 1 hour 24 minutes.

Question 8

The speed of a boat in still water is 8 km/h, and the speed of the stream is 2.5 km/h.

Part A: Find the time taken to travel 63 km downstream.

Step 1: Find downstream speed.

$$ 8+2.5=10.5\text{ km/h} $$

Step 2: Calculate time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{63}{10.5} $$

Answer: 6 hours.

Part B: Find the time taken to travel 22 km upstream.

Step 1: Find upstream speed.

$$ 8-2.5=5.5\text{ km/h} $$

Step 2: Calculate time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{22}{5.5} $$

Answer: 4 hours.

Question 9

Two boats P and Q have still-water speeds of 10 km/h and 14 km/h. At 8 a.m., P travels downstream and Q travels upstream from two places 96 km apart. The stream speed is 2 km/h. When will they meet?

Step 1: Find the downstream speed of boat P.

$$ 10+2=12\text{ km/h} $$

Step 2: Find the upstream speed of boat Q.

$$ 14-2=12\text{ km/h} $$

Step 3: Calculate their combined speed.

They travel towards each other, so add their speeds.

$$ 12+12=24\text{ km/h} $$

Step 4: Calculate the meeting time.

$$ \text{Time}=\frac{96}{24}=4\text{ hours} $$

They start at 8 a.m.

$$ 8\text{ a.m.}+4\text{ hours}=12\text{ noon} $$

Answer: 12 noon.

Question 10

A boat travels 40 km upstream in 5 hours. If the speed of the current is 2 km/h, find the speed of the boat in still water.

Step 1: Calculate upstream speed.

$$ \text{Upstream Speed}=\frac{40}{5}=8\text{ km/h} $$

Step 2: Calculate the boat's still-water speed.

$$ \text{Upstream Speed}=\text{Boat Speed}-\text{Stream Speed} $$

Therefore:

$$ 8=u-2 $$ $$ u=8+2 $$

Answer: 10 km/h.

10. Quick Revision Sheet
Situation	Formula or Rule
Train crosses a pole	Distance = Train length
Train crosses a bridge	Distance = Train length + Bridge length
Train crosses a platform	Distance = Train length + Platform length
Speed	Distance ÷ Time
Distance	Speed × Time
Time	Distance ÷ Speed
Same-direction relative speed	Difference of speeds
Opposite-direction relative speed	Sum of speeds
Downstream speed	Boat speed + Stream speed
Upstream speed	Boat speed − Stream speed
Boat speed in still water	(Downstream + Upstream) ÷ 2
Stream speed	(Downstream − Upstream) ÷ 2
km/h to m/s	Multiply by 5/18
m/s to km/h	Multiply by 18/5
11. Common Mistakes to Avoid
Forgetting the train's length: When crossing a bridge, add both lengths.
Using the wrong relative speed: Subtract speeds for the same direction; add them for opposite directions.
Mixing units: Convert km/h to m/s when distances are in metres and times are in seconds.
Confusing upstream and downstream: Downstream is addition; upstream is subtraction.
Forgetting to convert minutes: Convert minutes into hours before using speed in km/h.
Writing no units: Always include km, m, hours, seconds, km/h or m/s as appropriate.
12. Practice Questions for Students

Try these questions after completing the notes.

A train 240 m long crosses a pole in 12 seconds. Find its speed in m/s and km/h.
A train travels at 54 km/h and crosses a pole in 20 seconds. Find its length.
A train 120 m long crosses a bridge 180 m long at 15 m/s. Find the time taken.
Two trains travel in the same direction at 70 km/h and 50 km/h. Find their relative speed.
A boat travels at 12 km/h in still water. The stream speed is 3 km/h. Find its upstream and downstream speeds.
A boat covers 36 km downstream at 9 km/h. Find the time taken.
A boat's downstream speed is 18 km/h and its upstream speed is 12 km/h. Find its still-water speed and stream speed.
A student is 10 minutes late at 5 km/h and 10 minutes early at 7 km/h. Find the distance between home and school.
Answer Key
Question	Answer
1	20 m/s; 72 km/h
2	300 m
3	20 seconds
4	20 km/h
5	Upstream: 9 km/h; downstream: 15 km/h
6	4 hours
7	Still-water speed: 15 km/h; stream speed: 3 km/h
8	\(35/6\) km, or approximately 5.83 km

Teaching suggestion: Teach train-crossing questions first, then relative speed, followed by boats and streams. Finish with late-and-early questions, which require students to form an equation. This sequence moves from basic formulas to more challenging applications.

notes.title: Elements, Compounds and Mixtures
notes.contentHtml:
1. What Is Matter?

![](https://res.cloudinary.com/czb80riv/image/upload/v1792044570/studysathi/uploads/onfm9yleets775drxk3n.jpg)

Definition: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space.

Examples:

Water
Air
Books
Stones
Milk
Wood

Easy explanation: Anything that has weight and takes up space is called matter.

For example, a book has mass and occupies space, so it is matter.

Quick Tip

Remember two important things about matter:

It has mass.
It occupies space.
2. Classification of Matter

Matter can be classified into two main groups:

A. Pure Substances

Pure substances have a fixed composition and characteristic properties.

They are divided into:

Elements
Compounds

Examples: Pure copper, oxygen and distilled water.

B. Mixtures

A mixture is formed when two or more substances are physically combined.

Examples: Air, seawater, soil and snack mixtures.

Important Point

Distilled water is a pure substance, but it is a compound, not an element.

3. Elements
Definition

An element is a pure substance made of only one kind of atom.

It cannot be broken down into simpler substances by ordinary chemical methods.

| Rule 1 | True / Applicable | Requires Condition |
| Rule 2 | Always Valid | Exception at 0 |
Examples of Elements
Element	Chemical Symbol
Hydrogen	H
Oxygen	O
Carbon	C
Sodium	Na
Potassium	K
Iron	Fe
Calcium	Ca
Zinc	Zn
Sulphur	S
Mercury	Hg
Easy Explanation

Think of an element as a substance made from just one type of building block.

For example, pure iron contains iron atoms.

Quick Tips
An element contains one kind of atom.
Each element has a chemical symbol.
The first letter of a symbol is always capital.
If there is a second letter, it is lowercase.

Example: Co and CO mean different things. Co is the symbol for cobalt, while CO is the formula for carbon monoxide.

4. Compounds
Definition

A compound is a pure substance formed when two or more different elements chemically combine in a fixed proportion.

Examples
Compound	Chemical Formula	Elements Present
Water	H₂O	Hydrogen and oxygen
Carbon dioxide	CO₂	Carbon and oxygen
Sodium chloride	NaCl	Sodium and chlorine
Easy Explanation

Water is made from hydrogen and oxygen that are chemically combined.

Water has properties different from those of hydrogen and oxygen.

Important Properties of Compounds
They contain two or more different elements.
The elements are chemically combined.
The elements are present in a fixed proportion.
Their properties differ from those of their constituent elements.
They cannot be separated by simple physical methods.
Quick Tip

Compound = Different elements + Chemical combination + Fixed proportion.

5. Mixtures
Definition

A mixture is formed when two or more substances are physically combined without forming a new substance.

Examples
Air
Soil
Salt water
Seawater
Rice puffs mixed with peanuts and raisins
Properties of Mixtures
They contain two or more substances.
The substances are physically combined.
Their composition can vary.
The components generally retain their own properties.
They can often be separated by physical methods.
Methods of Separating Mixtures
Method	Example
Handpicking	Separating stones from rice
Filtration	Separating sand from water
Evaporation	Obtaining salt from salt water
Sieving	Separating larger particles from smaller particles
Magnetic separation	Separating iron filings from sand
Quick Tip

A mixture can often be separated by physical methods because its components are not chemically combined.

6. Types of Mixtures

Mixtures are mainly classified into two types: homogeneous and heterogeneous.

6
A. Homogeneous Mixture

Definition: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout.

This means the mixture is the same throughout, and its different components are not visibly distinguishable.

Examples:

Salt solution
Sugar solution
Air
Vinegar
Brass

Easy explanation: When salt dissolves completely in water, the salt solution looks the same throughout.

B. Heterogeneous Mixture

Definition: A heterogeneous mixture does not have a uniform composition throughout.

Its different components or regions may be distinguishable.

Examples:

Soil
Muddy water
Oil mixed with water
Rice puffs mixed with peanuts and raisins

Easy explanation: When oil and water are mixed, they form separate layers. Therefore, the mixture is heterogeneous.

Quick Comparison
Homogeneous Mixture	Heterogeneous Mixture
Uniform composition	Non-uniform composition
Components are not visibly distinguishable	Components or regions may be distinguishable
Example: Salt solution	Example: Muddy water
Example: Air	Example: Soil
Easy Memory Trick
Homo = Same
Hetero = Different
7. Other Important Terms
A. Solution

A solution is a homogeneous mixture.

Example: Salt water.

B. Alloy

An alloy is a mixture containing a metal and one or more other elements.

Examples:

Brass
Bronze
C. Colloid

A colloid is a mixture containing tiny dispersed particles.

Examples:

Milk
Fog
D. Suspension

A suspension is a heterogeneous mixture whose particles may settle when left undisturbed.

Example: Muddy water.

These definitions and examples follow your uploaded notes.

8. Pure Substance vs Mixture

This is an important comparison for examinations.

Pure Substance	Mixture
Has a fixed composition	Composition can vary
Contains one element or one compound	Contains two or more substances
Has characteristic properties	Properties depend on its components and proportions
Has definite melting and boiling points under a given pressure	May melt or boil over a range of temperatures
Cannot be separated into its components by ordinary physical methods	Components can often be separated by physical methods
Example: Pure copper	Example: Air
Quick Tip

Remember these four words:

Pure substance: Fixed composition.

Mixture: Variable composition.

9. Case Studies from the Chapter
Case Study 1: Box 1

The box contained crystals that looked similar in shape and colour.

Even after crushing, the smaller pieces looked similar.

Samples from different places were described in the story as having the same taste.

Conclusion: The intended conclusion in the textbook is that Box 1 contains a pure substance.

Case Study 2: Box 2

The box contained:

Rice puffs
Peanuts
Cornflakes
Raisins
Salt crystals

The components looked different and could be separated by hand.

Conclusion: Box 2 contains a heterogeneous mixture.

Comparison
Box 1	Box 2
Similar-looking crystals	Different snack ingredients
Pieces looked similar after crushing	Components remained distinguishable
No distinct components were visible to pick out	Components could be separated by hand
Intended conclusion: Pure substance	Heterogeneous mixture

Safety Tip: Never taste unknown substances in a laboratory or classroom. Use teacher-approved observation methods only.

10. Important Scientists and Their Contributions

Leucippus	Associated with early ideas that matter is made of tiny particles

Quick Memory Tips
Democritus: Atomos.

Dalton: Atomic Theory.

These are the key historical contributions listed in your uploaded notes.

11. Why Is Water a Compound?

Water has the chemical formula H₂O.

It contains hydrogen and oxygen chemically combined in a fixed ratio.

Therefore, water is a compound, not a mixture.

What Happens When Water Freezes?

When water freezes into ice, it remains H₂O.

When ice melts into water, it also remains H₂O.

These are physical changes because the state changes, but the substance remains the same.

What Is Electrolysis?

Electrolysis is a process in which electricity is used to decompose water into hydrogen and oxygen gases under suitable conditions.

Safety: Electrolysis requires appropriate equipment and teacher supervision. Never use a household power supply or an open flame near the gases produced.

12. Quick Revision Sheet

Pure substance	A material with fixed composition and characteristic properties

14. Answer Key
A. Very Short Answers

B. Key Points for Short Answers
A pure substance has fixed composition, characteristic properties, definite melting and boiling points under a given pressure, and cannot be separated into its components by ordinary physical methods.
A pure substance has fixed composition, while a mixture has variable composition. A pure substance may be an element or compound, while a mixture contains physically combined substances. Mixtures can often be separated physically, unlike pure substances.
Box 1 was intended to represent a pure substance because the crystals appeared similar. Box 2 was a heterogeneous mixture because its different components could be identified and separated.

questions.prompt: What is the formula for speed?
questions.explanation: Speed is calculated by dividing distance by time.

questions.prompt: A car travels 120 km in 3 hours. Find its speed in km/h.
questions.explanation: Speed = Distance ÷ Time = 120 ÷ 3 = 40 km/h.

questions.prompt: Convert 72 km/h into m/s.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 5/18: 72 × 5/18 = 20 m/s.

questions.prompt: Convert 25 m/s into km/h.
questions.explanation: Multiply by 18/5: 25 × 18/5 = 90 km/h.

questions.prompt: A cyclist travels at 20 km/h for 90 minutes. How far does the cyclist travel in kilometres?
questions.explanation: 90 minutes = 1.5 hours. Distance = 20 × 1.5 = 30 km.

questions.prompt: A train travels 495 km in 4 hours 30 minutes. What is its speed?
questions.explanation: 4 hours 30 minutes = 4.5 hours. Speed = 495 ÷ 4.5 = 110 km/h.

questions.prompt: A man runs at 10 km/h. How many minutes does he take to cover 750 metres?
A car travels equal distances at 60 km/h and 90 km/h. What is its average speed?
questions.explanation: For equal distances, average speed = 2xy/(x+y) = 2×60×90/150 = 72 km/h.

questions.prompt: Average speed is always total distance divided by total time.
questions.explanation: Average speed is defined as total distance travelled divided by total time taken.

questions.prompt: A truck covers 450 km in 9 hours. Find its average speed in km/h.
questions.explanation: Average speed = 450 ÷ 9 = 50 km/h.

questions.prompt: A 150 m train crosses a pole in 12 seconds. What is its speed in m/s?
questions.explanation: Speed = train length ÷ time = 150 ÷ 12 = 12.5 m/s.

questions.prompt: A train travels at 72 km/h and crosses a pole in 15 seconds. Find the train's length in metres.
A train 180 m long crosses a pole in 9 seconds. How long will it take to cross a 270 m bridge?
questions.explanation: Speed = 180 ÷ 9 = 20 m/s. Total distance = 180 + 270 = 450 m. Time = 450 ÷ 20 = 22.5 s.

questions.prompt: Two objects move in the same direction at 70 km/h and 50 km/h. What is their relative speed?
questions.explanation: For the same direction, subtract speeds: 70 − 50 = 20 km/h.

questions.prompt: A boat's speed in still water is 8 km/h and the stream speed is 2.5 km/h. What is its downstream speed?
questions.explanation: Downstream speed = boat speed + stream speed = 8 + 2.5 = 10.5 km/h.

questions.prompt: A boat's speed in still water is 7 km/h. It travels 22 km upstream in 4 hours. What is the stream speed?
questions.explanation: Upstream speed = 22 ÷ 4 = 5.5 km/h. Stream speed = 7 − 5.5 = 1.5 km/h.

questions.prompt: A boat travels 40 km upstream in 5 hours. The stream speed is 2 km/h. Find the boat's speed in still water.
questions.explanation: Upstream speed = 40 ÷ 5 = 8 km/h. Still-water speed = 8 + 2 = 10 km/h.

questions.prompt: When a boat moves downstream, the speed of the stream is added to the speed of the boat in still water.
questions.explanation: Downstream speed = still-water boat speed + stream speed.

questions.prompt: A shopkeeper buys a pair of shoes for \( \text{Rs. } 800 \) and sells them for \( \text{Rs. } 1000 \). What is the percentage profit earned by the shopkeeper?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the Cost Price (CP) and Selling Price (SP). CP = \( \text{Rs. } 800 \), SP = \( \text{Rs. } 1000 \).
Step 2: Calculate the Profit. Profit = SP - CP = \( 1000 - 800 = 200 \).
Step 3: Calculate the percentage profit using the formula: \( \text{Profit \%} = \left( \frac{\text{Profit}}{\text{CP}} \right) \times 100 \).
Step 4: Substitute the values: \( \text{Profit \%} = \left( \frac{200}{800} \right) \times 100 = \frac{1}{4} \times 100 = 25\% \).
Therefore, the percentage profit is 25%.

questions.prompt: The population of a town increased from 45,000 to 54,000 in one year. What is the percentage increase in the population?
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Identify the initial population and final population. Initial = 45,000, Final = 54,000.
Step 2: Calculate the increase in population. Increase = Final - Initial = \( 54,000 - 45,000 = 9,000 \).

Step 4: Substitute the values: \( \text{Percentage Increase} = \left( \frac{9,000}{45,000} \right) \times 100 = \frac{1}{5} \times 100 = 20\% \).
Therefore, the percentage increase is 20%.

articles.title: ISRO Chandrayaan & Space Science Explorations
articles.description: How Indian scientists explore lunar craters, solar winds with Aditya-L1, and future deep-space missions.
articles.content:
### Exploring the Cosmos with ISRO
India's space program has made historic breakthroughs that directly connect to our Class 8 physics and celestial studies.

#### 1. Why Study the Moon's South Pole?
The South Pole contains permanently shadowed craters where temperatures drop below $-200^\circ\text{C}$. In these cold traps, water ice remains preserved from billions of years ago.

#### 2. Key Science Takeaways for Class 8:
* **Gravity on Moon:** The Moon's gravitational acceleration is roughly $\frac{1}{6}$th of Earth's gravity ($g_{\text{moon}} \approx 1.62\text{ m/s}^2$).
* **Absence of Atmosphere:** Sound waves cannot propagate on the Moon because sound requires a material medium to travel.
* **Solar Power in Space:** Rovers use solar panels because there is no cloud cover to block solar radiation during lunar daytime.

articles.title: Modern Drip Irrigation & Micro-Sensors in Agriculture
articles.description: Agricultural scientists invent automated moisture sensors to save up to 60% irrigation water in Indian farms.
articles.content:
### Smart Irrigation in ICSE Class 8
In Chapter 1 (Crop Production and Management), we study traditional vs modern methods of irrigation.

#### Drip Irrigation (Trickle Method):
Water falls drop by drop directly near the roots of the plants through narrow pipes and emitters.

#### Why is it the most water-efficient method?
1. **Zero Evaporation Loss:** Water goes directly to the root zone instead of standing in open fields.
2. **Weed Prevention:** Unwanted weeds between rows don't get water to grow.
3. **Ideal for Water-Deficit Regions:** Highly recommended for regions with fruit gardens, orchards, and limited groundwater.

articles.title: The Science of Friction: Why Roller Bearings Prevent Energy Loss
articles.description: Investigating how rolling friction is significantly less than sliding friction in machines, bicycles, and skateboards.
articles.content:
### Friction: A Necessary Evil
In our physics syllabus, we learn that while friction causes wear and tear in machine parts, it is also essential for walking and holding objects.

#### Rolling vs Sliding Friction:
When an object rolls across a surface, the area of contact is minimal at any instant. Therefore:
$$\text{Rolling Friction} < \text{Sliding Friction} < \text{Static Friction}$$

#### Practical Application:
In ceiling fans and bicycle hubs, ball bearings replace sliding motion with rolling motion, dramatically reducing heat and mechanical friction!
